transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi… yeah. I’m here because I’ve been having this problem where I can’t seem to stay seated when I’m supposed to. Like during client interviews, or when I’m tutoring, or even at book club—which is ridiculous, because the whole point is to sit there and talk about the book. But I’ll keep getting up, pacing, grabbing water, checking something, and people are starting to notice that I’m not just sitting and listening like everyone else.
Do you feel anxious or on edge when you're in these situations where you can't stay seated?

I don’t know if I’d call it anxious, exactly. Maybe sometimes I feel… keyed up? But not like I’m scared something bad is going to happen. It’s more that sitting still starts to feel impossible, like my body wants to do something. 

I mean, in my work I’ve had plenty of actual anxious moments—surveillance in a bad neighborhood, awkward interviews, that sort of thing—and this doesn’t feel like that. Though now that I say it, maybe people noticing me makes me a little self-conscious. But the getting up part seems to happen before I’m even thinking about that.
Do you feel like you're getting up and pacing because you have to, or because you just can't sit still?

It’s more that I just can’t sit still. Like, I’ll tell myself, “Stay put, this is a client interview,” and then somehow I’m up getting water or pacing near the door. Same thing when I tutor, or even at book club—where, honestly, there’s no reason to be popping up every ten minutes. People have started noticing, which is embarrassing, but the urge to get up is already there before I’m thinking about that.
Do you have any recurring thoughts that you can't stop thinking about?

Not really… I mean, I have things I get stuck thinking about, like cases or whether I forgot to send someone an email, but I don’t think it’s like a recurring thought I can’t stop. My mind jumps around a lot more than it loops, if that makes sense.

Although now I’m thinking about this one book club argument we had about whether the narrator was reliable, and I did keep replaying that afterward—but that was more because I had a good point and didn’t make it clearly. So… no, I don’t think I have that kind of recurring thought.
Do you feel like you're doing these things, like pacing or getting up, in response to a specific urge or ritual?

Not a ritual, no. I don’t have some rule like I have to touch the doorframe or walk a certain number of steps or anything like that.

It’s more… I’m supposed to be sitting there listening—like in a client interview, or when I’m tutoring, or even at book club—and then I’m just up. Getting water, pacing a little, moving around like I need to do something. Which is ridiculous at book club, because nobody needs me to investigate the cheese plate. But people are starting to notice that I can’t just sit and listen, and that’s kind of what made me think, okay, this is becoming a problem.
Are you finding it harder to do your job or participate in social activities because of this inability to sit still?

Yeah… it is. I wish I could say it’s just annoying, but it’s starting to cost me at work.

I’ve missed details in investigations because I’m up moving around instead of just staying with what someone’s saying, and clients can tell I’m not settled. Some of them get irritated, like they think I’m rushing them or not taking them seriously. And with the junior detectives—this is embarrassing—I think they’re less willing to debrief with me now because I come in too fast, pacing, interrupting the flow, kind of steamrolling them without meaning to.

Socially it’s more awkward than catastrophic, but professionally, yes, it’s becoming a real problem.
How much distress or discomfort do you feel when you're unable to sit still in these situations?

It’s pretty uncomfortable, honestly. Not like panic exactly, but it’s this pressure of—okay, I’m supposed to stay put, I know I’m supposed to be listening, and then my body is already halfway out of the chair.

That’s really what brought me in. I keep getting up when I’m meant to stay seated—client interviews, tutoring sessions, even book club, which should be the easiest place to just sit there with wine and opinions. And people are noticing now. I can tell they’re watching me instead of just continuing the conversation, and then I get embarrassed, which somehow makes me want to move even more.
Are you having difficulty completing tasks or meeting deadlines at work due to your inability to sit still?

Yes… not always in a neat “deadline missed” kind of way, but it’s definitely interfering with finishing things properly.

Like, I’ll be in an interview and I get up, move around, go refill coffee—honestly, sometimes I think I’m being helpful, like when my aunt used to host people and couldn’t sit for more than two minutes, but that’s not the point. The point is I miss details. And in my work, a missed detail isn’t small. It can change the whole read on a case.

Clients get irritated too, because they can tell I’m not settled. They think I’m rushing them, or not listening closely enough. And the junior detectives… I think they’re less willing to debrief with me now because I come in pacing and talking over the rhythm of the conversation, like I’m pushing them along. I don’t mean to steamroll them, but that’s how it lands.

So, yes. It’s starting to cost me professionally.
Are your relationships with friends or family being affected by your inability to sit still?

Yeah, a bit. I mean, with friends it shows up more than family, I think—like book club, which is funny because it’s supposed to be relaxed, right? You sit, you talk about the book, someone brings those little crackers I always say I’m not going to eat and then I eat half the bowl—

But yes, people notice. I keep getting up when I’m supposed to just stay put and listen. Same kind of thing happens in tutoring sessions too, and obviously client interviews are worse because there’s more at stake. With friends, it’s more like they give me that look, like, “Are you leaving? Are you bored?” And I’m not bored. I just can’t seem to stay in the chair.
Do you feel like your inability to sit still is affecting your overall quality of life?

Yes. I mean, I’d like to say it’s just annoying, like some quirky “can’t sit through a meeting” thing, but it’s starting to feel bigger than that.

Professionally, especially. I’ve missed details in investigations because I’m up and moving around when I should be really locked in. And clients get irritated—they read it like I’m rushing them or not taking them seriously. Even the junior detectives seem less willing to debrief with me lately because I come in pacing and pushing the conversation along, and I think they feel steamrolled.

So… yeah, it’s affecting my life. It’s not ruining everything, but it’s costing me in ways I can’t really brush off anymore.
Are there any situations where you're able to sit still without feeling the urge to get up and pace?

Not really—at least not when I’m supposed to be sitting and listening. That’s the part that brings me in, honestly. I keep getting up at the wrong times: client interviews, tutoring sessions, even book club, which should be easy because it’s just friends and snacks and people arguing about whether the ending was “earned”—sorry, that’s not really the point.

The point is, if I’m expected to stay put and just listen, I start popping up. I’ll pace, refill water, adjust something, find a reason to move. And people notice. It’s not like I’m trying to leave or be rude, but I can’t seem to just sit there like everyone else.
Do you experience these urges to get up and pace at all times or just during specific situations?

It’s more in specific situations, I think—when I’m expected to stay put and just listen. Like client interviews, tutoring sessions, book club… those are the big ones.

I mean, I’m not pacing every second of the day. If I’m already moving around for work, that’s different. But when I’m supposed to be in a chair, attentive, not interrupting the flow—then I start getting this urge to get up. I’ll find some reason, like getting water or checking something, and then suddenly I’m standing again. People are starting to notice that I can’t just sit there like everyone else.
Are you feeling overwhelmed or stressed by your inability to sit still in these situations?

Yes, I do feel stressed by it. It’s sort of… embarrassing, honestly. What brings me in is that I keep getting up when I’m supposed to stay put—client interviews, tutoring sessions, even book club, which is ridiculous because nobody’s grading me there.

And then I start thinking, are they noticing? Are they annoyed? Do I look unprofessional? At book club last week—well, not last week, maybe two weeks ago—we got into this whole side argument about translations, and I got up three times to “check the tea,” even though the tea was fine. That’s the kind of thing I mean. I can’t just sit and listen, and people are starting to notice, so yes, it’s becoming overwhelming.
Are you feeling like your inability to sit still is significantly interfering with your ability to function at work or in social situations?

Yes. I mean, I don’t want to make it sound like everything is falling apart, because I’m still doing my job, but it’s definitely starting to cost me professionally.

In investigations, I’ve missed details because I was up pacing or moving around instead of just staying put and absorbing what someone was saying. And clients can get irritated—fairly, probably—if they feel like I’m restless during an interview. It gives the wrong impression, like I’m impatient with them.

And with the junior detectives, that’s been… uncomfortable. Some of them don’t really want to debrief with me as much because they feel like I steamroll the conversation. Which is funny, not funny, because I don’t mean to—I think I’m just trying to keep the energy moving, and then suddenly I’ve taken over. So yes, it’s interfering. Not catastrophically, but enough that people are reacting to it.
Do you think your inability to sit still is affecting your relationships with family members?

I’m not sure, honestly. Family is… a little harder for me to judge, because the roles are different, you know? At work there’s this clear expectation to sit still and be professional, and with friends or family it’s messier.

I don’t think anyone in my family has sat me down and said, “Your pacing is ruining dinner,” or anything like that. I mean, sometimes I’ll get up during a conversation to put dishes away or check something, and then I realize I’ve sort of wandered out of the moment. But whether that’s affecting the relationship, I don’t know. Families also just have their own habits—my mother used to clean during every phone call, so maybe I come by some of it honestly.

So… I guess I haven’t noticed a major effect with family members specifically. Not the way I have at work or in groups.
Do you often worry about things that are coming up in the future?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way. I mean, I plan for things—cases, appointments, whatever’s on the calendar—but “worry” feels a little broad.

Future things are funny, because in my line of work half the job is anticipating what might go wrong, but then that spills over into normal life sometimes… like I’ll be thinking about whether I remembered to buy coffee filters, and then somehow I’m reorganizing the whole week in my head. But is that worry? I don’t know.

So… no, I haven’t really noticed that I’m often worrying about the future in a big way. At least not as the main problem.
Do you often find yourself feeling nervous or on edge when you're not actively engaged in an activity or movement?

Yes, I think so. It’s less like I’m sitting there thinking, “I’m nervous,” and more like if I’m not actively doing something, my body starts looking for the next thing.

Like on days when I don’t have field work, I’ll tell myself I’m going to take it easy, and then suddenly I’m unpacking boxes, then reorganizing old case files, then I remember an errand, and I’m out the door like I’m chasing a lead. Which is ridiculous, because sometimes it’s just dry cleaning or buying tape.

So… yes, being still or off duty doesn’t really feel natural. I wouldn’t always call it anxiety, exactly, but I do feel kind of on edge if there isn’t some activity to plug into.
Did you experience significant symptoms of inattention or hyperactivity during childhood?

Yes, I did. I mean, looking back, it was there pretty early. My grade-school report cards always had some version of, “She’s bright, but she can’t stay in her seat,” or “needs to wait her turn,” which—honestly, those comments were so consistent they were practically part of the grading system.

My mother still jokes that I treated every classroom like a crime scene I had to pace through. Which is funny now, sort of, though I’m sure it was less funny for my teachers. I’d be up, looking around, interrupting, needing to move before I even realized I was doing it. So… yes, childhood, definitely.

But whether that’s affecting the relationship, I don’t know. Families also just have their own habits—my mother used to clean during every phone call, so maybe I come by some of it honestly.

So… I guess I haven’t noticed a major effect with family members specifically. Not the way I have at work or in groups.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are better explained by anxiety
doctor.question: Do you often worry about things that are coming up in the future?

target_item.reason: The question is about future-oriented worry/anxiety, which is not covered by the listed ADHD hyperactive/impulsive symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d put it that way. I mean, I plan for things—cases, appointments, whatever’s on the calendar—but “worry” feels a little broad.

Future things are funny, because in my line of work half the job is anticipating what might go wrong, but then that spills over into normal life sometimes… like I’ll be thinking about whether I remembered to buy coffee filters, and then somehow I’m reorganizing the whole week in my head. But is that worry? I don’t know.

So… no, I haven’t really noticed that I’m often worrying about the future in a big way. At least not as the main problem.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are better explained by anxiety
doctor.question: Do you often find yourself feeling nervous or on edge when you're not actively engaged in an activity or movement?

target_item.name: Constant_Activity
target_item.manifestation: On days when I don't have field work, I still move from unpacking boxes to reorganizing case files to running errands like I'm chasing a lead, and I have a hard time just being off duty.
target_item.reason: The question asks about feeling uncomfortable or on edge when not actively engaged in activity or movement, which most directly relates to being constantly active or driven to keep moving.

patient.answer:
Yes, I think so. It’s less like I’m sitting there thinking, “I’m nervous,” and more like if I’m not actively doing something, my body starts looking for the next thing.

Like on days when I don’t have field work, I’ll tell myself I’m going to take it easy, and then suddenly I’m unpacking boxes, then reorganizing old case files, then I remember an errand, and I’m out the door like I’m chasing a lead. Which is ridiculous, because sometimes it’s just dry cleaning or buying tape.

So… yes, being still or off duty doesn’t really feel natural. I wouldn’t always call it anxiety, exactly, but I do feel kind of on edge if there isn’t some activity to plug into.

doctor.question: Did you experience significant symptoms of inattention or hyperactivity during childhood?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: My grade-school report cards always said I was bright but couldn't stay in my seat or wait my turn, and my mother still jokes that I treated every classroom like a crime scene I had to pace through.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether significant ADHD symptoms were present during childhood, which directly corresponds to onset prior to age 12.

patient.answer:
Yes, I did. I mean, looking back, it was there pretty early. My grade-school report cards always had some version of, “She’s bright, but she can’t stay in her seat,” or “needs to wait her turn,” which—honestly, those comments were so consistent they were practically part of the grading system.

My mother still jokes that I treated every classroom like a crime scene I had to pace through. Which is funny now, sort of, though I’m sure it was less funny for my teachers. I’d be up, looking around, interrupting, needing to move before I even realized I was doing it. So… yes, childhood, definitely.
